slides.heading: How Quantum Error Correction Works
slides.body: The technology keeping quantum computers from falling apart

slides.heading: The Problem: Quantum Fragility
slides.body: Quantum bits (qubits) are extraordinarily sensitive — heat, vibration, or even a stray photon can flip their state. This 'decoherence' destroys calculations before they finish, making raw qubits nearly unusable for complex tasks.

slides.heading: Why Classical Fixes Don't Work
slides.body: Classical computers copy bits for redundancy. Quantum mechanics forbids copying unknown quantum states — the 'no-cloning theorem.' Measuring a qubit to check it instantly destroys the superposition you're trying to protect.

slides.heading: Encoding One Qubit in Many
slides.body: The solution: spread one logical qubit across many physical qubits using entanglement. Errors affecting a few physical qubits leave detectable patterns without revealing the protected information itself.

slides.heading: Syndrome Measurement
slides.body: Special 'ancilla' qubits measure relationships between data qubits — not the data itself. These measurements yield an error 'syndrome' that identifies what went wrong and where, without collapsing the logical qubit's state.

slides.heading: The Surface Code
slides.body: Google and IBM favor the surface code: qubits arranged in a 2D grid with data qubits at corners and ancilla qubits between them. It tolerates error rates up to ~1% and only needs nearest-neighbor connections — ideal for chip fabrication.

slides.heading: The Overhead is Enormous
slides.body: A fault-tolerant logical qubit may require 1,000 to 10,000 physical qubits depending on error rates. Running Shor's algorithm to break RSA-2048 encryption would need millions of physical qubits — far beyond today's hundreds.

slides.heading: The Threshold Theorem
slides.body: If physical error rates fall below a specific threshold (~1% for surface codes), adding more qubits improves reliability exponentially. This theorem proves fault-tolerant quantum computing is theoretically achievable — the race is hitting that threshold.

slides.heading: Recent Breakthroughs
slides.body: In 2024–2025, Google's Willow chip demonstrated that increasing code distance reduced errors exponentially — the first real-world validation of error correction scaling. IBM and Microsoft are pursuing alternative approaches with promising early results.

slides.heading: The Road to Fault-Tolerant Quantum
slides.body: Quantum error correction is the bridge between noisy lab experiments and practical quantum computers. Solving it doesn't just make quantum faster — it makes it possible. The breakthrough era has begun.
